analysis.title: Balanced By Design: AI optimism and market caution
key_insights: Tom Record (co-PM, Fidelity World and Global Special Situations) says the range of potential market outcomes is unusually wide and conviction in any single scenario is difficult, so he favors a balanced portfolio.

2026 has seen sharp rotations between growth and value and between technology and traditional sectors, often with little change in the underlying prospects of individual businesses. These rotations at times overwhelmed the gains from stock selection.
The AI investment cycle depends increasingly on extraordinary spending, access to financing and power availability. The author compares the investment levels to previous technology booms.

AI revenues are growing, use cases are broadening and costs are falling. The debate is shifting from whether demand will materialise to whether the required infrastructure can be delivered at the anticipated pace.

The largest technology companies generate large cash flows. Other AI infrastructure builders depend heavily on external funding, so higher borrowing costs or lenders' concentration limits could make some projects uneconomic and reduce demand across the supply chain.
The author says the brakes on AI investment may come from East Coast lenders who decide they hold enough datacentre risk, not from West Coast technology executives who decide to slow down.

A slowdown in infrastructure spending would not necessarily undermine AI's long-term success. Lower costs could make AI more affordable and speed adoption, but could pressure less competitive datacentre operators and create a more disinflationary environment for associated equipment and services.

The macro backdrop includes substantial government deficits, bond yields that have risen from exceptionally low levels, persistent inflationary pressures, higher energy costs, geopolitical uncertainty and changing trade relationships.
US midterm elections and growing political opposition to datacentre development could add constraints on infrastructure expansion.
The author is cautious on parts of the AI investment cycle where growth depends on continued access to financing, but keeps conviction in the long-term AI opportunity.

The portfolio combines businesses across investment styles and avoids dependence on a single market outcome. The author says a contrarian pessimistic or optimistic view is not rewarded in the current environment.

sector_views.rationale: Cautious on segments that depend on external financing, power availability and planning approvals. The long-term AI opportunity is still supported.

risk_factors: Financing risk for AI infrastructure builders if borrowing costs rise or lenders' concentration limits are reached.
Power availability and planning constraints on datacentre buildout.
Overinvestment in AI, with the author comparing it to the internet cycle.
Substantial government deficits, rising bond yields, persistent inflation and higher energy costs.
Geopolitical uncertainty, changing trade relationships and US midterm election politics, including opposition to datacentre development.
Style and sector rotations that overwhelm stock selection.
vol_and_positioning: Rapid rotations between growth and value and between technology and traditional sectors occurred through 2026, often with little change in company fundamentals.
geopolitical: Geopolitical uncertainty and changing trade relationships are cited as part of the economic backdrop.
US midterm elections and growing political opposition to datacentre development are cited as a possible constraint on infrastructure expansion.

tension_points.bull_case: AI revenues are growing, successful use cases are broadening, costs are falling and adoption is faster than in earlier technology cycles. Leading technology companies are substantially more profitable than in past booms.
tension_points.bear_case: The cycle depends on extraordinary spending, external financing and power availability. Higher borrowing costs or lender concentration limits could make some projects uneconomic, with overinvestment as in the internet cycle.

theme_stances.key_argument: The brakes on AI investment may be applied by lenders who decide they have enough datacentre risk, not by technology executives.
theme_stances.evidence: applied not by West Coast technology executives who decide to slow down

theme_stances.key_argument: Conviction in companies does not require certainty about markets, and a contrarian view is not rewarded now.
theme_stances.evidence: conviction in companies doesn't require certainty about markets
